title: Axial Muscles of the Head, Neck, and Back

## Overview

**Axial muscles** attach to the axial skeleton — the skull, vertebral column, and rib cage — and position the head, neck, and trunk. This topic surveys the axial muscles of the head, neck, and back, which fall into functional families: **muscles of facial expression** (move the skin of the face; facial nerve, CN VII), **muscles of mastication** (move the mandible; trigeminal nerve, CN V), **muscles of the tongue**, **extrinsic eye muscles**, **muscles of the anterior neck** (including the hyoid muscles of swallowing), and **intrinsic muscles of the back** that extend, laterally flex, and rotate the spine and head.

A key organizing idea: facial expression muscles insert into skin, not bone, which is why they can wrinkle a forehead or lift a smile; the intrinsic back muscles insert on bone and act like guy-wires holding the spine upright.

## Why This Matters

These muscles run your most visible and most vital behaviors. Facial expression muscles are the machinery of emotion — and their failure is a cardinal sign in conditions like Bell's palsy (facial weakness on one side). Mastication and tongue muscles are essential for eating and speaking; the hyoid muscles position the larynx during swallowing, directly relevant to aspiration risk. Neck muscles hold up a head that weighs several kilograms and are frequent sites of strain. The intrinsic back muscles keep you upright against gravity all day, and dysfunction here is central to low back pain — one of the most common reasons people seek healthcare.

## Core Concepts

### Muscles of facial expression

These thin muscles originate on skull or fascia and insert into the **skin** of the face; all are innervated by the **facial nerve (CN VII)**. Key players:

- **Epicranius** — the scalp muscle with two bellies: **frontalis** (raises eyebrows, wrinkles forehead) and **occipitalis** (back of skull), joined by the flat **galea aponeurotica**.
- **Orbicularis oculi** — the ring around the eye; closes the eyelid (blinking).
- **Orbicularis oris** — the ring around the mouth; closes and purses the lips.
- **Buccinator** — the deep cheek muscle that presses the cheek against the teeth during chewing.
- **Zygomaticus major and minor** — cheekbone to mouth corner; pull it up and back — the smile muscles.
- **Platysma** — a broad neck sheet that pulls the lower lip down and tenses the neck skin.

### Muscles of mastication

These move the mandible during chewing; all are innervated by the mandibular division of the **trigeminal nerve (CN V3)**:

- **Masseter** — the thick muscle at the cheek angle; the main elevator of the mandible (clenching).
- **Temporalis** — the fan-shaped muscle over the side of the skull; elevates and retracts the jaw.
- **Medial pterygoid** — elevates and protrudes the mandible, working with the masseter.
- **Lateral pterygoid** — opens the mandible, protrudes it, and moves it side to side; alternating pterygoids produce chewing's grinding motion.

### Muscles of the tongue

The tongue has **intrinsic muscles** (within it, shaping it) and **extrinsic muscles** (anchored outside, moving it) — **genioglossus** (protrudes), **styloglossus** (retracts/elevates), **hyoglossus** (depresses) — all innervated by the **hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)**, the nerve of tongue movement.

### Extrinsic eye muscles

Six small muscles rotate the eyeball: four **recti** and two **obliques** — the recti move it side to side and up and down; the obliques rotate it. Innervation is a classic exam question: lateral rectus = **CN VI (abducens)**, superior oblique = **CN IV (trochlear)**, the other four = **CN III (oculomotor)**.

### Muscles of the anterior neck

- **Hyoid muscles** attach to the hyoid bone, the small U-shaped bone anchoring the tongue and larynx. **Suprahyoid muscles** (digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid, geniohyoid) lie above and elevate it, positioning the larynx during swallowing; **infrahyoid muscles** (sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid) lie below and depress it. Their coordination is essential for safe swallowing and speech.
- **Sternocleidomastoid** — the strap from sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process; one side tilts the head and rotates the face to the opposite side; both sides flex the neck. It also assists inspiration.
- **Scalenes** — three muscles from the cervical vertebrae to the first two ribs; they laterally flex the neck and elevate the ribs during deep inspiration.

### Intrinsic muscles of the back

These deep muscles run along the vertebral column and act on the spine and head:

- **Splenius capitis and cervicis** — the most superficial intrinsic neck/back muscles; extend the head and neck and rotate them to the same side.
- **Erector spinae** — the great vertical column on either side of the spine, with three parallel columns: **iliocostalis** (lateral), **longissimus** (middle), and **spinalis** (medial). Together they extend the spine (standing up from a bent-over position); one side alone laterally flexes it.
- **Transversospinales** — deeper muscles running obliquely between vertebral processes: **semispinalis**, **multifidus**, **rotatores**. They extend and rotate the spine; the multifidus stabilizes individual segments.



## ELI-10: Explain Like I'm 10

Some of your muscles are attached to your skin instead of your bones — that's how you can smile, frown, and raise your eyebrows. Other muscles, like the strong ones in your cheeks and back, are attached to bones and do the heavy lifting: chewing, holding your head up, and keeping your spine straight. Neck muscles also help you swallow safely so food doesn't go down the wrong pipe.

## High-Yield Points

- **Facial expression muscles insert into skin** and are all innervated by **CN VII (facial nerve)**; damage → facial weakness (e.g., Bell's palsy).
- **Mastication muscles move the mandible** via **CN V3**: masseter and temporalis elevate; lateral pterygoid opens, protrudes, grinds.
- **Extrinsic tongue muscles: CN XII (hypoglossal)**.
- **Eye muscle mnemonic:** CN VI = lateral rectus, CN IV = superior oblique, CN III = the rest.
- **Hyoid muscles:** suprahyoid elevate, infrahyoid depress the hyoid/larynx (swallowing). Sternocleidomastoid: one side tilts/rotates; both sides flex the neck.
- **Erector spinae** (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis) extend and laterally flex the spine.
- **Transversospinales** (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores) rotate and stabilize spinal segments.

## Key Terms

| Term | Plain-Language Definition | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| axial muscles | Muscles attached to the axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, rib cage) | Position the head, neck, and trunk |
| epicranius | Scalp muscle with frontalis and occipitalis bellies joined by the galea aponeurotica | Raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead |
| buccinator | Deep cheek muscle that presses the cheek against the teeth | Keeps food between the teeth while chewing |
| masseter | Powerful muscle that elevates the mandible | The main clenching muscle |
| pterygoid muscles | Medial and lateral deep jaw muscles | Elevate/open/protrude the mandible and grind side to side |
| genioglossus | Extrinsic tongue muscle from the chin | Protrudes the tongue (CN XII) |
| suprahyoid / infrahyoid | Hyoid muscles above / below the hyoid bone | Position the hyoid and larynx for swallowing and speech |
| sternocleidomastoid | Neck strap from sternum + clavicle to mastoid process | Tilts/rotates the head; both sides flex the neck |
| erector spinae | Three-column back group (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis) | Extends and laterally flexes the spine; holds you upright |
| transversospinales | Deep back muscles (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores) | Rotate and stabilize spinal segments |

## How It Works / Step-by-Step Process

**Tracing a smile:** (1) motor cortex signals down CN VII; (2) branches reach the zygomaticus muscles; (3) the zygomaticus major pulls the mouth corner up and back as the orbicularis oculi tightens, crinkling the eyes; (4) the skin moves because these muscles insert into it, not bone.


## Example

**A swallowing checkpoint.** You take a sip of water. The suprahyoid muscles (mylohyoid, geniohyoid, digastric, stylohyoid) contract, lifting the hyoid bone and larynx upward and forward, helping close the airway and guiding the bolus into the esophagus. The infrahyoid muscles then gently lower the hyoid and larynx back to rest, while the tongue — pushed by the genioglossus and shaped by its intrinsic muscles — moves the water backward. If the cranial nerves controlling these muscles are impaired (as can happen after a stroke), coordination fails and aspiration risk rises — a direct clinical reason this muscle group matters.

## Common Confusions

| Do Not Confuse | With | Difference |
|---|---|---|
| Muscles of facial expression | Muscles of mastication | Expression muscles move skin (CN VII); mastication muscles move the mandible (CN V3) |
| Buccinator | Masseter | Buccinator compresses the cheek; masseter elevates the jaw |
| Suprahyoid muscles | Infrahyoid muscles | Suprahyoid elevate the hyoid/larynx; infrahyoid depress them |
| Erector spinae | Transversospinales | Erector spinae extend; transversospinales rotate and stabilize |
| Splenius rotation | Sternocleidomastoid rotation | Splenius rotates to the same side; sternocleidomastoid to the opposite side |
| Lateral rectus nerve | Superior oblique nerve | Lateral rectus = CN VI; superior oblique = CN IV; the rest = CN III |

## Quick Review

1. Which cranial nerve innervates all muscles of facial expression, and why do these muscles insert into skin?
2. Name the four muscles of mastication and the nerve that drives them.
3. What is the difference between suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles, and what do they do together?
4. Which back muscle group is the main extensor of the vertebral column, and what are its three columns?
5. Which nerves innervate the lateral rectus and the superior oblique eye muscles?
6. Contracting the right sternocleidomastoid alone produces what movement of the head?

<details>
<summary>Show answers</summary>

1. The facial nerve (CN VII). They insert into facial skin, so contraction creates expressions.
2. Masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, and lateral pterygoid — all innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).
3. Suprahyoid muscles lie above the hyoid and elevate it (and the larynx); infrahyoid muscles lie below and depress it. Together they position the larynx for safe swallowing.
4. The erector spinae group — its three columns are iliocostalis, longissimus, and spinalis.
5. Lateral rectus: abducens (CN VI). Superior oblique: trochlear (CN IV).
6. It tilts the head to the right and rotates the face to the left (opposite side).

</details>
